stem: A 24-year-old man with schizophrenia on an antipsychotic is seen drinking from the ward tap many times a day, about 6 L daily, and says he is not especially thirsty. Serum sodium is 120 mEq/L and urine osmolality is 80 mOsm/kg. He is then kept from fluids under supervision for several hours, followed by an injection of desmopressin.
oneliner: 24M + schizophrenia + drinking ~6 L/day + Na 120 + urine osm 80 + supervised water deprivation then desmopressin → plasma osm, urine osm, response?
ask: Which set of baseline plasma osmolality, urine osmolality after water deprivation and response to desmopressin is expected?

options.A: Plasma osmolality ↑; urine stays dilute after deprivation, concentrates after desmopressin
options.B: Plasma osmolality ↑; urine stays dilute after deprivation and after desmopressin
options.C: Plasma osmolality ↓; urine already concentrated before any deprivation
options.D: Plasma osmolality ↓; urine concentrates after deprivation, little further rise with desmopressin
options.E: Plasma osmolality normal; urine concentrates partly after deprivation, further after desmopressin

whyNot.A: This is **central diabetes insipidus**; the patient's sodium is **low**, so plasma osmolality is low, not high
whyNot.B: This is **nephrogenic diabetes insipidus**, where plasma osmolality is **high**; his sodium of 120 makes it low
whyNot.C: Concentrated urine with low plasma osmolality is **SIADH**; his urine is **maximally dilute** (80)
whyNot.E: A further rise after desmopressin marks **partial central DI**; his sodium is **120**, so plasma osmolality is low

answer: Low plasma osmolality; urine concentrates with deprivation; no extra response to desmopressin
why: He is drinking so much that plasma osmolality and sodium fall, **ADH is suppressed** and urine is dilute. When water is withheld, plasma osmolality climbs, **ADH is released** and the kidney concentrates urine normally, so desmopressin adds **little**. In DI, urine would stay dilute despite rising plasma osmolality.
chain: Dilute urine of 80 mOsm/kg and low sodium
Water deprivation lets plasma osmolality rise
ADH returns and urine concentrates; desmopressin adds little

idea.rule: Primary polydipsia: low plasma osmolality at baseline, but the ADH axis and kidney respond normally once water is restricted.
also: Central DI: high plasma osmolality; dilute urine corrected by desmopressin
Nephrogenic DI: high plasma osmolality; dilute urine not corrected by desmopressin
SIADH: low plasma osmolality with inappropriately concentrated urine
Beer potomania and tea-and-toast diets: low sodium from excess free water

stem: A 28-year-old man with fresh needle marks on both forearms comes in 12 hours after his last heroin use. He is yawning, restless and sweaty, with a runny nose and tearing, goose bumps, and crampy abdominal pain with loose stools. Pulse is 110/min.
oneliner: 28M + needle marks + 12 h since last heroin + yawning, rhinorrhea, piloerection, cramps, diarrhea + pulse 110 → which changes?
ask: Which set of changes is expected?

options.A: Pupils constricted, gut motility reduced, heart rate reduced
options.B: Pupils dilated, gut motility increased, heart rate increased
options.C: Pupils constricted, gut motility increased, heart rate increased
options.D: Pupils dilated, gut motility reduced, heart rate reduced
options.E: Pupils unchanged, gut motility reduced, heart rate reduced

whyNot.A: This is the **intoxicated** picture; his cramps, diarrhea and **pulse of 110** point the other way
whyNot.C: Gut and pulse fit, but **constricted pupils** belong to opioid effect, not withdrawal
whyNot.D: Dilated pupils fit, but **cramps and diarrhea** mean motility is up, and **110/min** is fast
whyNot.E: Against **loose stools and cramps**, and the **fast pulse** rules out a slowed heart

answer: Mydriasis, increased gut motility and tachycardia (opioid withdrawal)
why: Chronic **mu-receptor stimulation** held the **locus coeruleus** down; when the drug is gone, **noradrenergic output rebounds** and the gut loses its brake. The result is the **mirror image of intoxication**: dilated pupils, cramps with diarrhea and a fast pulse.
chain: Mu inhibition of the locus coeruleus is lost
Gut loses its brake: cramps and diarrhea

idea.rule: Withdrawal is the mirror image of the drug: what the drug turned down overshoots when it leaves.
also: Alcohol withdrawal: autonomic surge, tremor, tachycardia
Benzodiazepine withdrawal: anxiety, insomnia, seizures
Stimulant withdrawal: hypersomnia, hunger and low mood (the crash)
Nicotine withdrawal: irritability, increased appetite

stem: A 24-year-old man is found unresponsive at a party with a syringe beside him and a fresh puncture mark in his left antecubital fossa. Friends say he injected heroin about 20 minutes ago.
oneliner: 24M + found unresponsive + syringe + fresh injection mark + heroin 20 min ago → which changes?
ask: Which set of changes is expected?

options.A: Pupils dilated, respiratory rate increased, pulse increased, GCS decreased
options.B: Pupils constricted, respiratory rate increased, pulse increased, GCS normal
options.C: Pupils dilated, respiratory rate decreased, pulse decreased, GCS decreased
options.D: Pupils constricted, respiratory rate decreased, pulse decreased, GCS decreased
options.E: Pupils unchanged, respiratory rate decreased, pulse increased, GCS normal

whyNot.A: This is a **stimulant** pattern; **heroin** depresses breathing and pulse and shrinks the pupils
whyNot.B: Pupils fit, but **heroin** slows breathing and pulse, and he is **unresponsive**, so GCS cannot be normal
whyNot.C: Slow breathing and pulse fit, but a mu agonist after **heroin** gives **pinpoint**, not dilated, pupils
whyNot.E: He is **unresponsive**, so GCS is low, and heroin **slows** rather than speeds the pulse

answer: Miosis with slow breathing, bradycardia and reduced consciousness (opioid overdose)
why: Mu agonists **depress the brainstem**: respiratory centers lose sensitivity to CO2, the Edinger-Westphal nucleus is disinhibited so pupils become **pinpoint**, and vagal tone rises so the pulse slows. Sedation lowers the **Glasgow Coma Score**.
chain: Respiratory drive falls: rate slows, shallow

idea.rule: Pinpoint pupils with slow breathing and sedation = opioid until proven otherwise; miosis persists even in tolerant users.
also: Naloxone reverses miosis, respiratory depression and sedation
Tolerance develops to euphoria and respiratory depression, not to miosis or constipation
Pontine hemorrhage: pinpoint pupils with coma
Clonidine overdose: miosis, bradycardia and sedation

stem: An 82-year-old woman becomes confused two days after hip surgery. Her attention drifts in and out through the day and she is worse at night. A new sleep aid, diphenhydramine, was started after the operation.
oneliner: 82F + 2 days post hip surgery + fluctuating confusion, worse at night + new diphenhydramine → which neurotransmitter change?
ask: Which neurotransmitter abnormality is most likely implicated?

whyNot.B: Would give **parkinsonism**, not an acute fluctuating confusion; diphenhydramine does not block dopamine
whyNot.C: Gives **agitation, hyperthermia, clonus**; her new drug has no serotonergic action
whyNot.D: Not tied to **the new antihistamine**; low glutamate signaling is not the delirium model
whyNot.E: Her new drug **blocks** histamine receptors; the problem is not excess

answer: Reduced cholinergic activity in the brain
why: Delirium is linked to **low central cholinergic signaling**. **Diphenhydramine is strongly anticholinergic**, and older brains, already short of acetylcholine, tip over easily, giving an **acute, fluctuating** disturbance of attention.
chain: Old brain already low in acetylcholine

idea.rule: Anticholinergic load in the old can precipitate delirium; low acetylcholine is the working model.
also: Alzheimer disease: loss of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons
Donepezil raises acetylcholine for dementia
Benztropine, oxybutynin and tricyclics also provoke confusion in the old
Atropine toxicity: hot, dry, mad

stem: A 35-year-old man hears voices that tell him he is being followed. For months he has also had a blank face, very little speech, and has stopped washing or cooking for himself.
oneliner: 35M + persecutory voices + flat affect + poverty of speech + stopped self-care → which dopamine change explains the negative symptoms?
ask: Which dopamine pathway change best explains his flat affect and poor self-care?

options.A: Increased dopamine in the mesocortical pathway
options.B: Increased dopamine in the nigrostriatal pathway
options.C: Decreased dopamine in the tuberoinfundibular pathway
options.D: Increased dopamine in the mesolimbic pathway
options.E: Decreased dopamine in the mesocortical pathway

whyNot.A: Excess here would not produce **flat affect and avolition**; that is a deficit state
whyNot.B: Would cause **dyskinesias**, and nothing in the stem suggests movement disorder
whyNot.C: Low dopamine here raises **prolactin**; not his blank face and poor self-care
whyNot.D: Explains the **voices and persecution**, but not the flat affect or neglect

why: **Mesolimbic dopamine excess** produces the positive symptoms (voices, paranoia), while **low mesocortical dopamine** underlies the negative symptoms: **flat affect, alogia, avolition**. This is why D2 blockers help the first set and may not touch the second.
chain: Mesolimbic dopamine rises: voices and paranoia
D2 blockers fix the first, not always the second

idea.rule: Positive symptoms = too much mesolimbic dopamine; negative symptoms = too little mesocortical dopamine.
also: Nigrostriatal blockade: parkinsonism from antipsychotics
Tuberoinfundibular blockade: hyperprolactinemia
Mesolimbic: reward and psychosis
Second-generation antipsychotics add 5-HT2A block that may help mesocortical release
